abertura: You are at a conference in your field. The speaker is presenting results from a pilot programme.
Mark the two things that make a question, asked out loud, land well in a room like that.

itens.t: It points at something the speaker actually said.
It shows the room how much you know about the subject.
It names the part you are not sure about, and asks about that.
It is long enough that everyone can follow your reasoning.
It waits until the speaker has finished the whole talk.

sec1.rationale: A question that quotes the speaker back to herself is doing two things at once: it proves you followed, and it gives her something exact to answer.

nota.texto: The long question is the one that goes wrong most often, and it goes wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with English: by the time you reach the question mark, the room has stopped listening and the speaker is answering the first thing she remembers. Short is not modest — it is what gets answered.

nota.titulo: Two of these carry the talk
nota.texto:
Does that hold for…? is the whole question the man in the audience asks, and it is the most portable question in a conference room: it takes any claim and asks where its limit is.

And a different claim is the speaker's own point — not that the number is false, but that it answers a question nobody asked.

abertura: Six questions someone might ask after a talk. Say what each one is actually doing.
opcoes: asking where a claim stops being true
asking the speaker to repeat something
asking for something the talk did not cover

itens.t: "Does that hold for the second year as well?"
itens.ok: asking where a claim stops being true

itens.t: "Sorry -- was that sixty or sixteen?"
itens.ok: asking the speaker to repeat something

itens.t: "Do you have the same data for civil cases?"
itens.ok: asking for something the talk did not cover

itens.t: "You mentioned the cases were pre-selected -- selected by whom?"
itens.ok: asking where a claim stops being true

itens.t: "Are you sure you are not choosing the numbers that suit you?"
itens.ok: challenging the speaker's honesty

itens.t: "Could you go back to the slide before this one?"
itens.ok: asking the speaker to repeat something

nota.titulo: “Are you choosing the numbers that suit you?” is the one to avoid
nota.texto:
It may be exactly what you think. Said that way it stops being a question about the data and becomes a question about her — and the room hears the second one.

The same doubt, as a question about the claim: What would the figure be if the cases had not been pre-selected? Nobody has to defend themselves, and you still get your answer.

abertura: Two lines from the talk. Claire makes the same point twice, in two different ways.

audio.texto: What the slide does not say is which cases went into the pilot. They were the ones both sides had already agreed to send there.
I am not saying the pilot failed. I am saying we have a number that answers a different question from the one we asked.

abertura: Mark the two statements that match what she is arguing.

itens.t: The pilot programme failed.
The figure is real, but it answers a question nobody asked.
The cases in the pilot were not typical of all cases.
Ninety per cent is too high to be true.
The second year produced a worse programme.

sec4.rationale: She separates two things that sound like one: the figure is right, and it is evidence of something narrower than people take it for. She says so twice, in different words -- that repetition is the clue.

nota.titulo: Why this distinction is the lesson
nota.texto: Attacking the number is the easy move and it is usually wrong — the number is normally correct. What is wrong is what it is offered as evidence of. That distinction is the difference between an argument that survives and one that gets dismissed as scepticism.

abertura: This is how Marcus asked his, in the room. Listen once before you build yours.

audio.texto: You said the cases were pre-selected. Does that hold for the second year as well, or was that only the first round?

abertura: Each question starts by quoting the speaker. Complete it so that it asks about the claim, not about her.

itens.t: You said the cases were pre-selected --
alts: so the number is meaningless, isn't it?
why did nobody check that?
does that hold for the second year too?
itens.ok: does that hold for the second year too?

itens.t: You mentioned the figure drops to sixty-one --
alts: so the pilot did fail after all?
is that with the same definition of resolved?
how can both numbers be right?
itens.ok: is that with the same definition of resolved?

itens.t: I might be missing something, but
alts: that cannot possibly be correct.
what would the figure be without pre-selection?
surely you already knew that.
itens.ok: what would the figure be without pre-selection?

itens.t: Before I ask about the data --
alts: are these numbers yours or someone else's?
is any of this peer-reviewed?
can I check what counts as a case here?
itens.ok: can I check what counts as a case here?

nota.texto: Every one of these begins by giving the speaker back something she said. That is not politeness — it is what makes the question answerable. A question that starts from your own reasoning asks her to reconstruct it first, and in a room with forty people she will not.

nota.titulo: You will not read this in class
nota.texto: Writing it now is how the words become available later. In class you will ask a question out loud, in real time, without writing anything first — and that is the whole point of the lesson.

nota.titulo: “Does that hold for…?” is the kind that gets answered
nota.texto: All three kinds are legitimate. But a question that points at what she said hands her something exact to respond to, and one that points at her makes her defend herself before she answers anything. Same doubt, different room.

gs10d.rationale: She never disputes the number. She disputes what it is evidence of -- and she says it twice, in two different ways, which is how you know it is the point.

nota.titulo: Attacking the number is the wrong move
nota.texto: The number is almost always correct. What is wrong is what it is offered as evidence of — and that is the argument that survives.

askwell.titulo: Asking about a claim, not about a person
abertura: The same doubt, said three ways. Only one of them gets answered.

tabela:
You said the cases were pre-selected — does that hold for the second year?
She has something exact to answer. Nobody is defending anything.

Do you have the same data for civil cases?
Legitimate, but it leaves her claim untouched. Ask this second, not first.

Are you choosing the numbers that suit you?
Now the subject is her. The room hears the accusation and stops hearing the question.

callout.titulo: The three words that carry it
callout.texto: Does that hold… takes any claim at all and asks where its limit is, without implying the claim is false. It is the most portable question in a conference room, and it costs three words.
